title: 8 Rules That Built the VOC
dek: How quarrelling Dutch merchants created a new kind of company
cover_art_query: Vroom return second expedition East Indies
art_fallbacks: Dutch East India Company ships painting

slides.heading: Merge Your Rivals
slides.body: By 1601, rival Dutch companies were racing each other to Asia. They pushed pepper prices up there and down at home. The statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt forced them into one firm, chartered on 20 March 1602.

art.title: Portrait of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt
art.artist: Workshop of Michiel Jansz. van Mierevelt

slides.heading: Let Anyone Buy In
slides.body: Any resident of the Republic could subscribe, and more than a thousand people signed up in Amsterdam alone. Lodewijk Petram found Neeltgen Cornelis among them, a maid in the household of founder Dirck van Os. She put in 100 guilders.

slides.heading: Lock the Money In
slides.body: Earlier ventures were wound up after each voyage, with the cash and profits handed back. The VOC was meant to settle accounts after ten years, and in practice it never did. Permanent capital paid for forts, fleets and warehouses.
slides.art_query: East India House Amsterdam Oost-Indisch Huis

art.title: Binnenplaats van het Oost Indisch Huis te Amsterdam

slides.heading: Let the Shares Move Instead
slides.body: You couldn't take your money out, but you could sell your stake. Traders met in the street by the New Bridge, then in Hendrick de Keyser's new Exchange from 1611. Every sale was written into the company's ledger.
slides.art_query: Emanuel de Witte Amsterdam Exchange courtyard

slides.heading: Get Powers Like a State
slides.body: The charter gave the VOC a 21-year monopoly east of the Cape of Good Hope. It could also sign treaties, build forts, raise soldiers and appoint governors. A trading company with an army was the plan from day one.

slides.heading: Hire a Brilliant Lawyer
slides.body: In 1603 Jacob van Heemskerck seized the Portuguese carrack Santa Catarina and its cargo, worth millions of guilders. The company asked young Hugo Grotius to justify keeping it. One chapter became *Mare Liberum*, a classic of international law.

art.title: Château de Chantilly, Michiel van Mierevelt, portrait Hugo Grotius

slides.heading: Pay Out, Even in Spices
slides.body: Investors waited eight years for a first dividend. When it finally came in 1610, much of it was paid in mace, the lacy red spice that wraps a nutmeg. Shareholders could keep the spice or sell it.

art.title: De terugkomst in Amsterdam van de tweede expeditie naar Oost-Indië

slides.heading: Expect Shareholders to Bite Back
slides.body: Isaac Le Maire, a former director, complained about how the company was run in 1609 and organised a bet on falling share prices. In 1610 the States General answered with one of the earliest bans on short selling.

caption:
Seventeen gentlemen, six cities, one monopoly: the board that ran the Dutch East India Company.

The VOC had six chambers, and Amsterdam put up about half the money. That bought it eight of the seventeen board seats, while Zeeland had four. You will often read that it was the richest company ever, worth trillions in today's money. Treat that number as a modern guess. The boardroom fights were real.

Further reading: Lodewijk Petram, *The World's First Stock Exchange*; Femme Gaastra, *The Dutch East India Company*; Martine Julia van Ittersum, *Profit and Principle*

risk_notes: Richest company ever: the popular figure of about 7.9 trillion dollars is a modern estimate that historians don't stand behind. Keep it out of the slides. In comments, say it is often called the richest company in history, but that comparisons across centuries are rough guesses.

First joint-stock company or first stock exchange: the English East India Company (1600) and earlier Italian and Dutch partnerships came first. The slides avoid claiming 'first'. If pushed, say the VOC is the best-known early example of permanent, tradable share capital.
Neeltgen Cornelis: this comes from Petram's reading of the Amsterdam subscription register. If challenged, say 'according to the subscription register studied by Lodewijk Petram'.

Permanent capital: the charter planned a general settlement after ten years, but it was put off and the capital became permanent in practice. In 1612 the directors chose not to pay it out. Say 'in practice' when asked.
Short-selling ban: the February 1610 decree banned selling shares you did not own (windhandel). Call it 'one of the earliest' bans, not definitely the first.

Grotius: *Mare Liberum* (1609) was taken from his longer unpublished manuscript *De Jure Praedae*. Van Ittersum shows the VOC was closely involved in having it written. Valuations of the Santa Catarina cargo vary (roughly 3 to 3.5 million guilders), so 'millions of guilders' is the safe wording.
1610 dividend: it was paid largely, not entirely, in mace. Keep the phrase 'much of it'.
